title: Etcd disk latency causing heartbeat throttling - postmortem draft
content:
Summary:

On 2024-11-02 at ~03:12 UTC we observed elevated API-server request latencies across multiple regions and a rise in pod scheduling failures followed by a cascade of control-plane warnings. Root cause analysis shows a sustained spike in disk write latency on etcd member nodes which caused etcd heartbeat RPCs to be delayed and leader heartbeats to be throttled, increasing leader election times and momentary API-server unavailability.

Impact:
- Duration: ~20 minutes of degraded control-plane responsiveness (03:12 - 03:32 UTC).
- Symptoms: kubectl commands timed out intermittently; controller-manager and scheduler observed leader election delays; some short-lived 5xx from hosted API components that issue frequent reads to kube API.
- Affected regions: us-west-2 primary etcd cluster (multi-az). No data loss detected; quorum maintained.

Detection timeline (high level):
- 03:11 UTC: Pager alert SRE-3241 triggered: etcd_peer_round_trip_time_p95 > 500ms.
- 03:12 UTC: Oncall (pager: Evan) confirmed API-server 5xx spike and increased scheduler eviction logs.
- 03:15 UTC: Ops runbook: collect etcd pod logs, top/dstat on etcd hosts, and check disk metrics.
- 03:18 UTC: Observed node-level block device write latency (iostat avg wait) increasing to 200-400ms on two etcd hosts.
- 03:20 UTC: A flurry of leader-change events in etcd logs; API-server reported grpc deadline exceeded to etcd.
- 03:26 UTC: Disk scheduler changes and temporary IO throttling mitigation applied (see mitigation).
- 03:32 UTC: Metrics recovered to baseline. Follow-up investigation started.

Immediate mitigations performed:
1) Isolate noisy process: On host etcd-03 we found an unrelated nightly backup job triggered on attached backup-volume which was performing synchronous fsync-heavy operations to a secondary mount. We stopped the backup process (systemctl stop nightly-backup).
2) Temporary IO policy: Adjusted cgroup blkio weight for etcd container to favor etcd IO (blkio.weight=800) while running recovery checks.
3) Evict/restart: We did not restart etcd processes to avoid forcing leader changes. Instead we relied on removing the noisy process and IO prioritization; quorum remained stable.

Root cause analysis (RCA):
- Immediate cause: High block device write latency on two etcd member hosts (etcd-02 and etcd-03) due to a combination of: (a) an accidental cron job that mounted and wrote to a backup volume with synchronous fsync semantics; (b) kernel writeback amplification on ext4 where the secondary mount shared the same physical device as the etcd data LVM.
- Contributing factors:
  - Storage topology assumption mismatch: backup volume was expected to be network-attached but was actually provisioned on the same NVMe as etcd data after a provisioning template change during an infra churn.
  - Lack of IO isolation: etcd containers had no enforced IO cgroup policy, relying on best-effort scheduling by host; user-space backup process consumed most of the I/O queue.
  - Alerting tuning: p95 peer RTT alert fired but had a relatively high threshold before pages; earlier degradation signs (disk latency) were visible in node exporter but not wired to a page.
- Why the leader heartbeat throttled: etcd's raft heartbeats are sensitive to RPC latency. When block IO latencies rose, write RPCs (append entries/heartbeats) experienced long RTTS and the leader deferred some operations, leading to leader election churn and timeouts at the API-server layer.

Logs and evidence (excerpts):
- etcd logs (etcd-02):
  Nov 02 03:19:14 etcd[pid]: warn grpc: failed to accept from 10.0.12.5: rpc error: code = DeadlineExceeded desc = context deadline exceeded
  Nov 02 03:20:01 etcd[pid]: info raft: 3 became leader at term 45
  Nov 02 03:20:02 etcd[pid]: warn raft: heartbeat took too long (took=590.132ms)

- Host metrics snapshot (iostat):
  Device: nvme0n1  r/s  w/s  rsec/s  wsec/s  await  svctm  %util
  03:15  1.2  12.1  150  12000   312.4  25.3   96.8

- kernel logs: repeated WAKEUP for process backup-worker and block layer timeouts.

Post-incident analysis details:
- We reconstructed storage layout via lsblk and lvdisplay and confirmed the backup mount and etcd LV mapped to the same physical NVMe device on two nodes. This was the result of a storage provisioning script change (infra PR #612) that repurposed ephemeral metadata volumes during a prior maintenance window.
- The backup job was configured to run daily at 03:00 and uses a program that issues direct fdatasync calls per file causing synchronous write amplification.

Why existing mitigations didn't prevent this:
- We lacked IO QoS for etcd containers on hosts.
- Backups are run as system services on hosts rather than scheduled in a controlled pool with storage guarantees; this coupling was not documented clearly in the provisioning template.
- The alerting runbook emphasized CPU/memory pressure for etcd but did not have a direct page for sustained block latency above X ms on ectd hosts.

Action items (short/medium/long) - owner and ETA:
- Short (1 week):
  - Add a paging alert for block device write latency on etcd hosts (SRE) - owner: Evan Brooks - ETA: 2024-11-09.
  - Add runbook step to check for local backup/cronjobs on control-plane hosts during high etcd latency incidents - owner: Maya Patel - ETA: 2024-11-06.
- Medium (2-4 weeks):
  - Enforce blkio cgroup weights for etcd containers via systemd unit or kubelet static pods (SRE + Infra) - owner: Liam O'Connor - ETA: 2024-11-23.
  - Audit provisioning templates to ensure backup mounts are on physically separate devices or network storage (Infra) - owner: Sofia Ramirez - ETA: 2024-11-20.
- Long (1-3 months):
  - Move backup job to a dedicated backup fleet or convert to controller-run job that uses network storage (Platform) - owner: Platform Eng lead - ETA: 2025-01-15.
  - Investigate use of fio-based CI tests on storage provisioning flow to detect shared-device accidental mappings (SRE + Release Eng) - owner: Release Eng - ETA: 2025-01-31.

Runbook changes (explicit edits to keep in the SRE playbook):
- New checklist item under "etcd high-latency" playbook:
  1. Check node exporter -> node_disk_io_time_seconds or iostat for p95 write await > 50ms on etcd hosts.
  2. Run: lsblk && lvs && mount | grep etcd-data to confirm separate devices.
  3. If local backup process found: systemctl stop <backup-service> && check IO recovery metrics.
  4. If IO not recovering: consider moving one member to maintenance (evict from LB) after leader stepdown plan - avoid full restart if quorum fragile.
- Add sample kubectl/grafana queries to runbook:
  - kubectl get pods -n kube-system -l k8s-app=etcd -o wide
  - kubectl logs -n kube-system etcd-02 --tail=200
  - Grafana panels: etcd_server_proposals_committed_total, etcd_net_peer_round_trip_time_seconds_bucket (p95), node_disk_io_time_seconds_count and node_disk_io_time_seconds_sum to compute average await.

Follow-ups already in motion:
- Infra PR to update provisioning template to explicitly create separate block devices for etcd LVs (PR #789 open).
- SRE alerting PR to wire node exporter disk latency into a low-latency page.
- Scheduled knowledge-sharing with Platform and Backup owners to prevent host-level backup jobs from running on critical control-plane nodes.

Lessons learned (concise):
- EtcD is sensitive to block device performance; treat etcd members as a tier-0 workload requiring IO isolation and explicit QoS.
- Small ops changes (provisioning template tweak) can introduce surface area for large system-level regressions if the storage topology assumptions are not documented/validated.
- Observability matters: node-level disk signals should be part of control-plane SLO alerting and paging.

Appendix - useful commands and snippets used during triage:
- Check device mapping: lsblk -o NAME,SIZE,ROTA,MOUNTPOINT,LABEL
- Check LV mapping: sudo lvs -o lv_name,vg_name,lv_attr,devices
- Short iostat run: iostat -x 1 5 nvme0n1
- Inspect etcd peer RTT in Prometheus: rate(etcd_network_peer_round_trip_time_seconds_sum[1m]) / rate(etcd_network_peer_round_trip_time_seconds_count[1m])
- Example journalctl filter used: journalctl -u nightly-backup.service --since "2024-11-02 02:45" --until "2024-11-02 03:30"

Draft conclusion statement:
This incident was caused by accidental co-location of an fsync-heavy backup job onto the same physical devices as etcd data LVs, which produced elevated block device write latencies and delayed etcd raft heartbeats. No data loss occurred and quorum remained intact; impact was limited to control-plane latency and short-lived scheduling failures. The immediate mitigations avoided a forced restart and restored normal operation. Our next steps are to eliminate the storage topology mismatch, add IO isolation for etcd, and improve alerting/runbook steps to reduce time-to-detect and avoid recurrence.
